abstract: |
  Multicenter randomized trials require a choice among ignoring,
  fixing, or randomizing site effects in the primary analysis. We
  report a Monte Carlo simulation of this choice for a continuous
  outcome, structured under the ADEMP framework of Morris, White,
  and Crowther (2019). It varies the number of sites, the
  site-level variance, treatment-by-site interaction, and
  site-size balance. We compare OLS ignoring site, OLS with fixed
  site effects, and a random-intercept linear mixed model. For
  the interaction scenarios we add a random-slopes model.
  Mixed-model tests use Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. We
  report bias, standard errors, power, coverage, Type I error, and
  singular-fit rates, each with its Monte Carlo standard error.
  The study is a tutorial-style replication, and its main findings
  agree with earlier simulation studies. With about 20 patients
  per site and treatment balanced within site, the fixed-site and
  random-site models were indistinguishable. Ignoring site gave
  conservative inference, with Type I error well below the nominal
  level and lower power. Under treatment-by-site interaction, the
  fixed-site and random-intercept tests were anti-conservative for
  the super-population mean effect. They were close to nominal for
  the conditional effect in the sampled sites. The random-slopes
  model restored coverage and Type I error. However, it lost
  substantial power and returned frequent singular fits. Small
  centers, many sites, and low intraclass correlation, where the
  methods are known to differ, were not studied. Code for the
  simulation is provided.

# Introduction

Multicenter randomized clinical trials (RCTs) are the standard
design for confirmatory evaluation of therapeutic
interventions. These trials enroll participants across several
clinical sites. This lets them reach practical recruitment
targets. It also broadens the population base, which helps the
findings generalize [@iche9; @localio2001adjustments].
However, the multicenter structure brings several analytic
complications. If they are mishandled, they can distort
inference about treatment effects. In this paper we address
four related statistical issues. Each arises in the design and
analysis of multicenter RCTs with continuous outcomes. We
present simulation evidence on each issue in turn.

## Modeling site effects

The first question is how site (or center) effects should
enter the primary analysis. There are three broad strategies.
The first ignores site differences entirely. The second treats
sites as fixed effects. The third treats sites as random
effects drawn from a population of potential sites. Each
strategy carries its own assumptions. Each also has different
consequences for the validity and efficiency of treatment
effect estimation [@senn1998controversies; @jones1998comparison].

Localio and colleagues gave an influential overview of the
problem. They named three analytic challenges in multicenter
data: within-center correlation of outcomes, confounding by
center, and effect modification across centers
[@localio2001adjustments]. The choice between fixed and random
effects models has been debated at length. Fixed effects
models condition on the observed sites. They make no
distributional assumptions about site effects. However, they
use up degrees of freedom quickly when the number of sites is
large relative to the total sample size
[@pickering2007analysis]. Random effects models instead treat
site effects as draws from a normal distribution. This approach
estimates only a variance component, not individual site
parameters. Kahan and Morris found that it was at least as
efficient as fixed effects in the settings they studied
[@kahanmorris2013continuous]. We fit it with \texttt{lme4}
[@bates2015lme4]. ICH E9 treats mixed models more narrowly. It
describes them as a tool to 'explore the heterogeneity of the
treatment effect'. In such models 'centre and
treatment-by-centre effects' are random. E9 calls these models
'especially relevant when the number of sites is large'
[@iche9, Section 3.2]. The same section considers trials with
too few patients per center to model center effects. For those
trials it states that 'it is not appropriate to include a term
for centre in the model'.

Chu and colleagues ran a comprehensive simulation of six
analytic approaches for continuous outcomes. They varied the
number of centers, the center sizes, and the intraclass
correlation coefficient (ICC) [@chu2011comparing]. All methods
gave unbiased point estimates. However, ignoring centers
inflated the standard error when within-center correlation was
present. It also reduced power. The mixed-effects model
attained nominal coverage and near-optimal power in nearly all
configurations. Generalized estimating equations (GEE)
underestimated the standard error when there were few centers.

Kahan and Morris extended these findings. They showed that
random center effects performed at least as well as fixed
effects in every scenario they examined. Random effects did
substantially better when each center had few patients
[@kahanmorris2013continuous]. Islam and Bangdiwala confirmed
these patterns in a recent replication study. Their study
covered both continuous and binary outcomes. It supports
random effects models as a default analytic strategy
[@islam2024accounting].

## What does 'random' mean here?

Before going further, we need to be precise about the word
'random.' This word carries most of the weight in the
discussion above. It can mean two different things. We spell
out both meanings in plain terms, with the underlying
mathematics alongside. The two meanings lead to two different
arguments later in this Introduction.

### A hospital-specific shift, fixed or random

To illustrate, consider a trial run at ten hospitals. Each
hospital has its own typical outcome level. The reasons have
nothing to do with the treatment being tested. They include a
different mix of patients, different routine practices, and
different equipment. We call that hospital-specific shift
$\alpha_i$, for hospital $i$. We write $Y_{ij}$ for the
outcome of patient $j$ at hospital $i$. In symbols, a simple
model for that outcome is:

$$Y_{ij} = \alpha_i + \delta \, T_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij}$$

Here $T_{ij}$ is 1 if the patient received the active
treatment and 0 if not. The quantity $\delta$ is the treatment
effect the trial is designed to estimate. The term
$\epsilon_{ij}$ is ordinary patient-to-patient variation. It
has nothing to do with which hospital a patient attended.

But what kind of quantity is $\alpha_i$?

There are two options. The first treats each hospital's shift
as an ordinary fixed number. In kind it is no different from a
patient's age or sex. That is, it is something to adjust for,
with one number per hospital. Ten hospitals means ten fixed
numbers to estimate.

The second option treats $\alpha_i$ as random, drawn from a
normal distribution: $\alpha_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\alpha)$.
Under this option, the one unknown quantity of real interest
is $\sigma^2_\alpha$. That is, how much do hospitals
typically differ from one another? The analysis does not
estimate ten separate numbers. Instead it estimates a single
number that describes the *spread* of hospital effects.

This is not a small technical difference. It changes what the
analysis is entitled to claim. Estimating ten fixed numbers
tells us only about these ten specific hospitals. Estimating
one spread, $\sigma^2_\alpha$, is a broader claim. That is, it
says something about hospital-to-hospital variation in
general. It describes the variation we would expect if the
trial had, by chance, enrolled a different set of ten
hospitals.

That broader claim is exactly where a disagreement in the
published literature appears. We return to it below.

### Why the simulation redraws the site effects

The simulation draws new site effects
$\alpha_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\alpha)$ for every simulated
trial. This is needed for the performance measures to mean what
we intend. Coverage and power are then averaged over many
possible sets of sites, all with the same spread
$\sigma^2_\alpha$. A simulation that reused one fixed set of
site effects would assess each method only for those sites. The
interaction effects $\gamma_i$ and the imbalanced site sizes
are redrawn in the same way. This choice is a property of the
simulation design. It is not a claim about how real hospitals
are chosen for a real trial. That separate question is taken up
next.

### Two different reasons statisticians give for treating site as random

Everything so far concerns how the simulation is built. A
separate question concerns a real trial with real hospitals.
Why should an analyst treat site as random rather than fixed
when fitting the actual statistical model? Published
statisticians do not fully agree on the reason. They disagree
even where they agree on the recommendation. In our view a
statistically literate reader should know both arguments.

The first argument says the random-effects model literally
means what it appears to mean. That is, it treats the
hospitals in the trial as if they had been drawn at random
from a much larger population of possible hospitals. Falissard
and Chavance make this point directly. In their view the
random-effects interpretation is only truly justified when the
hospitals really were chosen at random from a wider population
[@falissard1996effet]. Unfortunately, in practice that is
almost never how hospitals are chosen. Hospitals join a trial
because they can recruit patients quickly. They may join
because an investigator has a relationship with the study team.
They may also join for reasons of funding and logistics. They
are not chosen by a lottery over all possible hospitals [@senn1998controversies].

The second argument does not depend on how the hospitals were
chosen at all. Kahan and Morris justify adjusting for site on
the design of the trial itself. Patients were randomly split
between treatment and control separately within each hospital.
As a result, the analysis should reflect that split. This holds
no matter how the hospitals themselves came to be in the trial
[@kahanImproperAnalysisTrials2012a;
@kahanmorris2013continuous]. Edgar, Roberts, and Sharples
reach a similar conclusion on practical grounds. They
re-analyzed CRASH-2, a trial with a binary outcome (death)
analyzed in 271 centers in 40 countries. They report that random
intercepts 'may increase power and decrease bias'
[@edgar2021including]. Their evidence comes from a binary
outcome, so it supports our continuous-outcome setting only
indirectly.

These two arguments do not agree on *why* a random site
effect is the right choice. However, they agree on *what to
do*. That is, prefer a random effect for site once there are
more than a handful of hospitals. The recommendation in this
paper rests on that agreement. It therefore stands regardless
of which argument a reader finds more convincing. We note that
the simulation itself is a super-population model. It draws
new site effects $\alpha_i$ for every simulated trial. A purely
design-based study would instead hold the sites fixed and
re-randomize only the treatment. Our performance measures are
therefore averages over both sites and randomizations. They do
not imply that real hospitals are a random sample of all
possible hospitals.

## Failure to adjust for stratification variables

The second issue concerns what happens when the analysis
ignores stratification variables, including site. In
multicenter trials it is standard to stratify randomization by
center. In that case, failing to adjust for the stratification
factor in the analysis leads to biased inference. Kahan and
Morris showed this through simulation. An unadjusted analysis
of a trial randomized with stratified blocks gives standard
errors that are biased upward. It also gives confidence
intervals that are too wide and Type I error rates below the
nominal level. Statistical power is lost as well
[@kahanImproperAnalysisTrials2012a]. This conservatism has a
simple source. Stratified randomization balances the arms
within each site. A shared site effect then enters both arm
means in the same way. As a result, the two arm means are
positively correlated. The unadjusted variance formula ignores
this covariance. It therefore overstates the variance of the
difference in means.

Kahan and Morris extended this work to trials with several
stratification factors. They found that adjusting for the main
effects of all stratification variables was generally enough.
Adjustment for all cross-classified strata was not required
[@kahanAdjustingMultiplePrognostic2013]. These findings agree
with ICH E9. It states that 'Factors on which randomisation has
been stratified should be accounted for later in the analysis'
[@iche9, Section 2.3.2]. It also states that 'If one or more
factors are used to stratify the design, it is appropriate to
account for those factors in the analysis' [@iche9, Section
5.7]. The findings also agree with current regulatory guidance
on covariate adjustment [@fda2023covariate]. Bugni, Canay, and
Shaikh gave the large-sample theory. They showed that the
two-sample $t$-test is conservative under covariate-adaptive
randomization [@bugni2018inference]. Ye and colleagues showed
how to adjust for the randomization strata and gain efficiency
[@ye2023toward].

## Treatment-by-site interaction

The third concern is heterogeneity of the treatment effect
across sites. Even under a common protocol, eligible
participants may vary. So may site practices and investigator
experience. The result is genuine treatment-by-site
interaction [@fedorov2005misleading]. Senn argued that some
degree of treatment-by-center interaction is inevitable in
practice. In his view a rational approach to planning
multicenter trials should anticipate it
[@senn1998controversies].

The ICH E9 guideline recommends a two-step approach. First,
fit a model without the interaction term to estimate the main
treatment effect. Then examine heterogeneity as a secondary
analysis. However, the power to detect treatment-by-site
interaction is typically low. As a result, a non-significant
interaction test does not establish homogeneity
[@sennlewis2019treatment]. Jones and colleagues compared three
kinds of estimator: fixed-effects weighted, unweighted, and
random effects. They did so under varying degrees of
treatment-by-center interaction [@jones1998comparison]. The
fixed effects weighted estimator performed well across a range
of interaction magnitudes. Unweighted estimators, on the other
hand, could be inefficient when site sizes differed markedly.

Treatment-by-site interaction may be modeled as random. That
is, the treatment slope may vary across sites. The mixed model
then estimates both the average treatment effect and the
variance of treatment effects across sites. This gives a
natural summary of heterogeneity [@neuhaus2006separating].

## Imbalanced site sizes

The fourth issue is closely related to the preceding three. It
is whether imbalance in site sizes affects inference.
Enrollment in multicenter trials is often highly unequal
across sites. In such trials, a few large sites contribute a
disproportionate share of participants. Senn noted that a
rational approach to planning multicenter trials leads
naturally to unequal site sizes. Sites with higher recruitment
capacity will enroll more patients within the trial's fixed
time window [@senn1998controversies].

Ruvuna introduced a coefficient of imbalance. It quantifies
the power loss due to unequal center sizes. He showed that
substantial imbalance can reduce power when an unweighted
(Type III) analysis is used [@ruvuna2004unequal]. Vierron and
Giraudeau formalized this through a design effect framework.
They showed that the efficiency loss depends on two
quantities. One is the ICC. The other is a statistic for the
heterogeneity of group distributions across centers
[@vierron2009design]. When the ICC is positive, balanced
allocation is optimal. However, moderate imbalance imposes
only a modest efficiency penalty. The key risk arises when
site size is informative. That is, larger sites may
systematically differ from smaller sites in patient
characteristics or treatment delivery. This could possibly
introduce bias into the treatment effect estimate
[@fedorov2005misleading; @agresti2000strategies].

## Present study

The existing literature gives clear guidance on each issue
separately. Chu and colleagues, Kahan and Morris, and Islam and
Bangdiwala have already compared ignoring, fixing, and
randomizing site by simulation. Islam and Bangdiwala also
reported Type I and Type II error rates
[@chu2011comparing; @kahanmorris2013continuous;
@islam2024accounting]. Our study is a tutorial-style
replication that places the four issues in one design. We do
not claim new findings for the main fixed-versus-random
comparison. The added elements are a treatment-by-site
interaction arm with a random-slopes model and a matching null
arm. We also report singular-fit rates throughout.

The simulation varies the number of sites, the site-level
variance, treatment-by-site interaction, and site-size
balance. It covers 16 of the 24 cells formed by these factors
(Methods, "Parameter values"). It evaluates bias, empirical
and model-based standard error, power, and coverage of 95\%
confidence intervals for the average treatment effect. Every
site has about 20 patients, with treatment balanced within
site. In this regime treatment is nearly orthogonal to site.
As a result, the fixed and random site models are expected to
agree closely. Earlier work finds that the methods differ with
small centers, many sites relative to $N$, and low ICC
[@pickering2007analysis; @kahanmorris2013continuous]. These
regimes are outside our grid.

# Methods

## ADEMP structure

Following Morris, White, and Crowther [-@morris2019using], we
report the simulation under the ADEMP framework.

- **Aims.** We compare three strategies for site heterogeneity:
  ignore site, fixed site effects, and random site effects. The
  scenarios vary the number of sites, the site variance,
  treatment-by-site interaction, and site-size balance. We also
  assess Type I error under a true null effect. For the
  interaction scenarios we add a fourth method, a random-slopes
  model.
- **Data-generating mechanism.** This is detailed in the next
  subsection.
- **Estimand.** The primary target is $\delta$, the mean of the
  super-population distribution of site-specific effects
  $\delta + \gamma_i$. It is a data-generating parameter with a
  known value, in the sense of Morris et al. With
  $\sigma^2_\gamma > 0$, the methods do not all target $\delta$.
  The fixed-site estimator targets a conditional quantity. That
  is, it targets a weighted mean of the realized effects
  $\delta + \gamma_i$ of the $K$ sampled sites. The weight of
  site $i$ is $n_{i1} n_{i0} / n_i$, where $n_{i1}$ and $n_{i0}$
  are its arm sizes. With unequal site sizes this is close to a
  patient-weighted average, not a site-weighted average
  [@kahan2023estimands]. We therefore also evaluate every method
  against this conditional target. Neither target is a full ICH
  E9(R1) estimand [-@iche9r1].
- **Methods.** Ignore site and fixed site effects are fit by OLS
  with \texttt{lm}. The random-intercept and random-slopes models
  are fit by REML with \texttt{lme4::lmer} [@bates2015lme4]. All
  four methods are fit to every replicate, so comparisons are
  paired. The random-slopes model is reported for the interaction
  scenarios and their null counterparts. Tests and 95\% CIs use a
  $t$ reference distribution. For the OLS methods its df is the
  residual df. For the two mixed models it is the Satterthwaite
  df from \texttt{lmerTest} [@kuznetsova2017lmertest]. Luke found
  that Satterthwaite and Kenward-Roger df both control Type I
  error well in small samples [@luke2017evaluating;
  @kenward1997small]. As a sensitivity analysis we repeat the
  mixed-model tests and CIs with $K - 1$ df.
- **Performance measures.** We report bias, empirical SE, MSE,
  mean model SE, power at $\alpha = 0.05$, and coverage of 95\%
  CIs. In the $\delta = 0$ scenarios, power is the Type I error
  rate. We also report the convergence rate and the
  singular-fit rate. Each measure has its Monte Carlo SE from
  Morris Table 6. Non-convergence is a hard error from
  \texttt{lmer}. A singular fit is a successful fit at the edge
  of the variance parameter space. We track these two outcomes
  separately for each scenario and method.

## Data generating model

For each simulated trial, we generate data from a two-level
model with patients nested within sites. Let $Y_{ij}$ denote
the continuous outcome for patient $j$ at site $i$. In
symbols,

$$Y_{ij} = \alpha_i + (\delta + \gamma_i) T_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij}$$

where $\alpha_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\alpha})$ is the
random site intercept, $\delta = 0.30$ is the true average
treatment effect, $\gamma_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\gamma})$
is the random treatment-by-site interaction,
$T_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}$ is the treatment indicator, and
$\epsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_e = 1)$ is the
residual error. Within each site, treatment is assigned by one
random permutation of a balanced 0/1 vector of length $n_i$.
This gives complete balance within every site, or a difference
of one when $n_i$ is odd. It is a single block per site, not a
sequence of permuted blocks.

## Parameter values

The simulation crosses the following factors:

- **Number of sites:** $K = 10$ (few) vs $K = 30$ (many)
- **Site-level variance:** $\sigma^2_{\alpha} \in \{0, 0.10, 0.50\}$
  (none, moderate, large)
- **Treatment-by-site interaction:**
  $\sigma^2_{\gamma} \in \{0, 0.04\}$ (none vs present)
- **Site size balance:** balanced ($n_i = 20$ for all $i$)
  vs imbalanced (see below)

```{r imbal-cv, include=FALSE}
# Realized CV and total N of the imbalanced site-size generator.
# Run before `sim-run`, which re-seeds the RNG itself, so these
# draws do not affect the simulation stream.
source(here::here("analysis/scripts/sim_multicenter.R"))
set.seed(20261117)
imbal_cv <- purrr::map_dfr(c(10, 30), function(k) {
  draws <- purrr::map(seq_len(5000), function(i) {
    as.numeric(table(generate_trial_data(
      k, 20, FALSE, 0, 0, 0, 1
    )$site))
  })
  tibble::tibble(
    K = k,
    cv = mean(purrr::map_dbl(draws, \(s) sd(s) / mean(s))),
    n = mean(purrr::map_dbl(draws, sum))
  )
})
```

Imbalanced site sizes are generated in four steps. Raw sizes
are drawn from a $\text{Gamma}(0.8, 0.8/20)$ distribution. They
are rounded and floored at 4. They are then rescaled to sum to
about $20K$, rounded, and floored at 4 again. The Gamma draw
alone has a coefficient of variation (CV) of about 1.1. The
flooring lowers it. Over 5,000 draws the realized mean CV was
`r sprintf('%.2f', imbal_cv$cv[imbal_cv$K == 10])` for $K = 10$
and `r sprintf('%.2f', imbal_cv$cv[imbal_cv$K == 30])` for
$K = 30$. The total $N$ is not fixed. Its mean was
`r sprintf('%.0f', imbal_cv$n[imbal_cv$K == 10])` and
`r sprintf('%.0f', imbal_cv$n[imbal_cv$K == 30])`, against
nominal values of 200 and 600.

The factors are not fully crossed. For each $K$ the grid omits
four of the twelve cells. These are imbalanced sizes with no
site variance, interaction with no site variance (balanced and
imbalanced), and interaction with moderate site variance and
imbalanced sizes. The null-hypothesis arm ($\delta = 0$)
repeats 14 of the 16 alternative cells. It omits only the
moderate-variance imbalanced cells. It includes the six
interaction cells. These allow us to assess the Type I error of
the random-slopes model.

The true treatment effect is $\delta = 0.30$ in the alternative
scenarios. This is 0.30 standard deviations of the residual
error ($\sigma_e = 1$). The total outcome SD is larger when
$\sigma^2_\alpha > 0$. For example, it is
$\sqrt{1.5} \approx 1.22$ when $\sigma^2_\alpha = 0.50$.

## Analytic methods

We analyze each simulated dataset by three primary methods.
A fourth method is also fit on every replicate, for a paired
comparison. We report it for the interaction scenarios and
their null counterparts (Results, "Random slopes under
treatment-by-site interaction"):

1. **Ignore site:** $Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T_{ij} + e_{ij}$
   (ordinary least squares, no site term)
2. **Fixed site effects:**
   $Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T_{ij} + \sum_{k=2}^{K} \beta_k I(i=k) + e_{ij}$
   (site indicators as fixed effects)
3. **Random site effects:**
   $Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T_{ij} + u_i + e_{ij}$
   where $u_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_u)$ (linear mixed model
   via REML)
4. **Random slopes:**
   $Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T_{ij} + u_i + v_i T_{ij} + e_{ij}$
   where $(u_i, v_i)$ jointly follow a bivariate normal
   distribution (random intercept and random treatment slope
   per site, via REML). This is the correctly specified model
   under the treatment-by-site-interaction data-generating
   mechanism (Data generating model, $\gamma_i$). Method 3, by
   contrast, omits the random slope and is misspecified
   whenever $\sigma^2_{\gamma} > 0$.

## Simulation procedure

```{r sim-run, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=tools::md5sum(here::here("analysis/scripts/sim_multicenter.R"))}
source(here::here("analysis/scripts/sim_multicenter.R"))

# The scenario grid lives in the script (build_scenarios()) so that
# the tinytest suite can check it. The six null-arm interaction rows
# are appended last, which leaves the RNG stream of the first 24
# scenarios unchanged.
scenarios <- build_scenarios()

# Morris, White, and Crowther (2019) 4.1: pin RNGkind and set the
# seed ONCE; run_simulation() consumes RNG state from this stream.
RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG")
set.seed(20260310)

raw_results <- run_simulation(
  scenarios, n_sim = 1500,
  rng_state_path = here::here(
    "analysis/data/derived_data/rng_states.rds"
  )
)
sim_summary <- summarize_simulation(raw_results)
# The Methods text states Satterthwaite df; the naive-df fallback
# never triggered in development and must not do so silently here.
stopifnot(all(sim_summary$df_fallback_rate == 0))

# Alternative (true_trt = 0.30) and null (true_trt = 0) arms are
# reported separately: coverage of a nonzero effect is not the same
# quantity as Type I error. The random-slopes method is kept out of
# Table 1, Table 2, and Figures 1 to 3, and is reported in Table 3.
sim_summary_alt <- dplyr::filter(
  sim_summary, true_trt > 0, method != "random_slope"
)
sim_summary_null <- dplyr::filter(
  sim_summary, true_trt == 0, method != "random_slope"
)
raw_results_alt <- dplyr::filter(
  raw_results, true_trt > 0, method != "random_slope"
)

# Random intercept versus random slopes, in the interaction
# scenarios (sigma_trt_site > 0) under the alternative and the null.
int_labels <- scenarios$label[scenarios$sigma_trt_site > 0]
sim_summary_slope_int <- dplyr::filter(
  sim_summary,
  scenario %in% int_labels, true_trt > 0,
  method %in% c("random_site", "random_slope")
)
sim_summary_slope_null <- dplyr::filter(
  sim_summary,
  scenario %in% int_labels, true_trt == 0,
  method %in% c("random_site", "random_slope")
)
```

We replicate each scenario $R = 1{,}500$ times. The Monte Carlo
SE of an estimated coverage or Type I error probability $p$ is
$\text{MCSE} = \sqrt{p(1-p)/R}$ (Morris, White, and Crowther
2019, Table 6). We evaluate this at the nominal $p = 0.95$.
This is the worst case among the coverage targets considered
here. At that value, $R \geq 1{,}320$ is required for MCSE
$\leq 0.6$ percentage points. We note that $R = 1{,}500$ gives
MCSE $\approx 0.56$ pp. This meets the target with a margin.
Treatment is assigned by balanced allocation within each site.
That is, each site has equal numbers of treatment and control
participants, or numbers within $\pm 1$ when $n_i$ is odd.
All random number generation uses a fixed seed
(\texttt{set.seed(20260310)}) and the \texttt{L'Ecuyer-CMRG}
RNG for reproducibility. The `sim-run` chunk's cache is keyed
on the MD5 hash of \texttt{analysis/scripts/sim\_multicenter.R},
in addition to the chunk's own text. This means that a change
to the simulation functions themselves, not just to this
chunk, correctly invalidates the cached result. The cache
cannot silently reuse output from a prior version of the
simulation code.

# Results

## Headline findings

```{r headline-07, include=FALSE}
# Key numbers for the prose, read from the `sim-run` objects.
hl_random <- sim_summary_alt |>
  dplyr::filter(method == "random_site") |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    power_min = min(power), power_max = max(power),
    cov_min = min(coverage), cov_max = max(coverage)
  )
hl_bias <- max(abs(sim_summary_alt$bias))
hl_ignore <- sim_summary_alt |>
  dplyr::filter(method == "ignore_site") |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    cov_min = min(coverage), cov_max = max(coverage),
    power_min = min(power)
  )
hl_fr <- sim_summary_alt |>
  dplyr::filter(method %in% c("fixed_site", "random_site")) |>
  dplyr::select(scenario, method, power, coverage, mcse_power) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = method, values_from = c(power, coverage, mcse_power)
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    d_power = max(abs(power_random_site - power_fixed_site)),
    d_cov = max(abs(coverage_random_site - coverage_fixed_site))
  )
hl_conv <- min(sim_summary$convergence_rate)
hl_sing <- sim_summary_alt |>
  dplyr::filter(method == "random_site") |>
  dplyr::mutate(novar = grepl("noVar", scenario)) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    novar_min = min(singular_rate[novar]),
    novar_max = max(singular_rate[novar]),
    other_max = max(singular_rate[!novar])
  )
```

We observe the following across the
`r nrow(sim_summary_alt) / 3` alternative-hypothesis scenarios
($\delta = 0.30$), each with $R = 1{,}500$ replications. Table 1
gives the Morris Table 6 Monte Carlo SEs in parentheses next to
the power and coverage estimates. The random-site mixed model
attained power between `r sprintf('%.2f', hl_random$power_min)`
and `r sprintf('%.2f', hl_random$power_max)`. Coverage of its
95\% confidence interval ranged from
`r sprintf('%.3f', hl_random$cov_min)` to
`r sprintf('%.3f', hl_random$cov_max)`. Absolute bias never
exceeded `r sprintf('%.3f', hl_bias)` for any method.

The fixed-site and random-site models were indistinguishable in
this grid. Their power differed by at most
`r sprintf('%.3f', hl_fr$d_power)` in any scenario. Their
coverage differed by at most `r sprintf('%.3f', hl_fr$d_cov)`.
This agreement follows from the design, as the Discussion
explains. Ignoring site produced overcoverage, up to
`r sprintf('%.3f', hl_ignore$cov_max)`. It also produced lower
power, as low as `r sprintf('%.2f', hl_ignore$power_min)`. Both
effects occurred when the site variance was non-zero.

The lowest convergence rate across all scenarios and methods
was `r sprintf('%.3f', hl_conv)`. This rate counts hard
\texttt{lmer} errors only. Singular fits are a separate matter.
With zero true site variance, the random-site model
returned a singular fit in
`r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * hl_sing$novar_min)` to
`r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * hl_sing$novar_max)`\% of replicates.
With positive site variance, the rate was at most
`r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * hl_sing$other_max)`\%. A singular fit
still returns a usable point estimate. However, its
variance-component estimate is degenerate. Type I error under
the null is reported in Table 2.

## Summary of performance metrics

    R = 1500 replications per scenario. `Sing.' is the

## Type I error under the null

Coverage of a 95\% CI centered on the true alternative
($\delta = 0.30$, Table 1) is one quantity. The Type I error
rate of the associated test under a true null effect
($\delta = 0$) is a different one. We note that Type I error
is the quantity most directly relevant to the stratified-
randomization literature that motivates this study
[@kahanImproperAnalysisTrials2012a;
@kahanAdjustingMultiplePrognostic2013]. Table 2 reports the
empirical rejection rate at $\alpha = 0.05$. It covers the 14
null-hypothesis scenarios described in Methods, including the
six with treatment-by-site interaction.

```{r results-table-null}
sim_display_null <- sim_summary_null |>
  mutate(
    scenario = str_remove(scenario, "^H0_") |>
      str_replace_all("_", " "),
    method = case_when(
      method == "ignore_site" ~ "Ignore",
      method == "fixed_site" ~ "Fixed",
      method == "random_site" ~ "Random"
    ),
    t1_mcse = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", power, mcse_power),
    coverage_mcse = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", coverage, mcse_coverage),
    singular = ifelse(
      method == "Random", sprintf("%.1f\\%%", 100 * singular_rate),
      "--"
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    Scenario = scenario, Method = method,
    Bias = bias, `Type I error (MCSE)` = t1_mcse,
    `Coverage (MCSE)` = coverage_mcse, Sing. = singular
  )

kable(
  sim_display_null,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  digits = 3,
  escape = FALSE,
  caption = "Empirical Type I error under the null hypothesis
    ($\\delta = 0$) at nominal $\\alpha = 0.05$, by scenario and
    analytic method, with Morris et al. (2019) Table 6 Monte Carlo
    SE in parentheses. R = 1500 replications per scenario. `Sing.'
    is the random-site singular/boundary-fit rate among converged
    fits.",
  linesep = ""
) |>
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("hold_position", "scale_down"),
    font_size = 8
  )
```

```{r t1-summary, include=FALSE}
t1 <- sim_summary_null |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    int = scenario %in% int_labels,
    z = (power - 0.05) / mcse_power
  )
t1_fr <- dplyr::filter(t1, method != "ignore_site")
t1_ig <- dplyr::filter(t1, method == "ignore_site")
t1_exc <- dplyr::filter(t1_fr, !int, z > 2)
t1_exc_cells <- unique(str_replace_all(
  str_remove(t1_exc$scenario, "^H0_"), "_", " "
))
t1_slope <- dplyr::filter(sim_summary_slope_null,
                          method == "random_slope")
cond_fixed <- dplyr::filter(
  sim_summary, scenario %in% int_labels, method == "fixed_site"
)
fmt_rng <- function(x, d = 3) {
  paste(sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), range(x)), collapse = " to ")
}
```

Consider first the null scenarios without interaction. There
the fixed-site and random-site tests had Type I error from
`r fmt_rng(t1_fr$power[!t1_fr$int])`. Ignoring site gave rates
from `r fmt_rng(t1_ig$power[!t1_ig$int])`. With site variance
present, these were up to
`r sprintf('%.0f', max(-t1_ig$z[!t1_ig$int]))` MCSEs below the
nominal 5\%. That is, ignoring site was markedly conservative.
This agrees with Kahan and Morris
[@kahanImproperAnalysisTrials2012a] and with Bugni and
colleagues [@bugni2018inference]. One cell stands out. In
`r paste(t1_exc_cells, collapse = ', ')`, the fixed-site and
random-site rates were
`r paste(sprintf('%.3f', t1_exc$power), collapse = ' and ')`.
These are about
`r sprintf('%.1f', min(t1_exc$z))` to
`r sprintf('%.1f', max(t1_exc$z))` MCSEs above nominal. The two
methods give nearly the same estimate on the same data. Their
excursions are therefore one event, not two. Among 16 such
comparisons one excursion of this size is not surprising. We
did not increase $R$ for this cell.

The null scenarios with interaction behave differently. There
the fixed-site and random-intercept tests rejected in
`r fmt_rng(t1_fr$power[t1_fr$int])` of replicates. Both models
omit the random slope. Their standard errors therefore do not
include the between-site variance of the treatment effect. As a
result, they are anti-conservative for $\delta$. This is partly
a question of estimand (Methods, "ADEMP structure"). Against its
own conditional target, the fixed-site interval covered in
`r fmt_rng(cond_fixed$coverage_cond)` of replicates, across all
twelve interaction scenarios. The random-slopes test had Type
I error from `r fmt_rng(t1_slope$power)`. Ignoring site gave
`r fmt_rng(t1_ig$power[t1_ig$int])`.

These results are specific to the scenarios simulated. The
random-site and random-slopes tests use a $t$ reference with
Satterthwaite df. A singular fit returns a valid estimate and
standard error. Unfortunately, its sampling distribution at the
boundary need not match that $t$ approximation.

## Random slopes under treatment-by-site interaction

The random-site method fitted throughout this report (Table 1,
Table 2) includes only a random intercept. This model is
misspecified for the six treatment-by-site-interaction
scenarios ($\sigma^2_{\gamma} = 0.04$). Those scenarios are
generated with a genuine random treatment slope, $\gamma_i$
(Data generating model). Table 3 compares the intercept-only
specification with the correctly specified random-slopes
method (Analytic methods, Method 4). Both are fit on the same
generated data. The comparison is restricted to those six
scenarios and their null counterparts.

```{r results-table-slope}
slope_t1 <- sim_summary_slope_null |>
  transmute(
    scenario = str_remove(scenario, "^H0_"), method,
    t1_mcse = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", power, mcse_power)
  )
sim_display_slope <- sim_summary_slope_int |>
  left_join(slope_t1, by = c("scenario", "method")) |>
  mutate(
    scenario = str_replace_all(scenario, "_", " "),
    method = case_when(
      method == "random_site" ~ "Random intercept",
      method == "random_slope" ~ "Random slope"
    ),
    singular = sprintf("%.1f\\%%", 100 * singular_rate),
    power_mcse = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", power, mcse_power),
    coverage_mcse = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", coverage, mcse_coverage)
  ) |>
  select(
    Scenario = scenario, Method = method,
    Bias = bias, `Emp. SE` = empirical_se,
    `Model SE` = mean_model_se,
    `Power (MCSE)` = power_mcse, `Coverage (MCSE)` = coverage_mcse,
    `Cov. ($K-1$ df)` = coverage_km1,
    `Type I (MCSE)` = t1_mcse,
    Sing. = singular
  )

kable(
  sim_display_slope,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  digits = 3,
  escape = FALSE,
  caption = "Random intercept versus random slopes for the six
    treatment-by-site-interaction scenarios ($\\sigma^2_{\\gamma} =
    0.04$), fit on the same generated data. Power, coverage, and
    Type I error use Satterthwaite df. `Cov. ($K-1$ df)' repeats
    the coverage calculation with $K - 1$ df. `Type I' is the
    rejection rate in the matching null scenario ($\\delta = 0$,
    same $\\sigma^2_{\\gamma}$). `Sing.' is the singular-fit rate
    among converged fits for that method; for Random slope it
    refers to the joint intercept-slope covariance parameter
    space.",
  linesep = ""
) |>
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("hold_position", "scale_down"),
    font_size = 8
  )
```

```{r slope-headline, include=FALSE}
sl_compare <- sim_summary_slope_int |>
  select(scenario, method, power, coverage, mean_model_se,
         mean_df) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = method,
    values_from = c(power, coverage, mean_model_se, mean_df)
  )
sl_cov_gain <- sl_compare$coverage_random_slope -
  sl_compare$coverage_random_site
sl_pow_loss <- sl_compare$power_random_site -
  sl_compare$power_random_slope
sl_k10 <- grepl("^K10", sl_compare$scenario)
sl_slope <- dplyr::filter(sim_summary_slope_int,
                          method == "random_slope")
sl_sing <- raw_results |>
  dplyr::filter(method == "random_slope",
                scenario %in% sim_summary_slope_int$scenario,
                !is.na(est)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    cover = abs(est - true_trt) <= stats::qt(0.975, df) * se
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(scenario, singular) |>
  dplyr::summarise(mdf = mean(df), cov = mean(cover),
                   .groups = "drop")
```

Table 3 shows both sides of a trade-off. On the plus side, the
random-slopes model had higher coverage than the misspecified
random-intercept model in all six scenarios. The gain ranged
from `r sprintf('%+.1f', 100 * min(sl_cov_gain))` to
`r sprintf('%+.1f', 100 * max(sl_cov_gain))` percentage points.
On the minus side, its power was lower in every scenario. The
loss ranged from `r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * min(sl_pow_loss))` to
`r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * max(sl_pow_loss))` points. It was
largest at $K = 10$. There it was at least
`r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * min(sl_pow_loss[sl_k10]))` points. Two
things widen the random-slopes interval. Its mean model SE was
larger. Its mean Satterthwaite df were also much smaller, from
`r sprintf('%.0f', min(sl_compare$mean_df_random_slope[sl_k10]))`
to `r sprintf('%.0f', max(sl_compare$mean_df_random_slope[sl_k10]))`
at $K = 10$.

The random-slopes model returned a singular fit in
`r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * min(sl_slope$singular_rate))` to
`r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * max(sl_slope$singular_rate))`\% of
replicates. Its df depend strongly on singularity. Non-singular
fits had mean df of `r fmt_rng(sl_sing$mdf[!sl_sing$singular], 0)`. Singular fits
had mean df of `r fmt_rng(sl_sing$mdf[sl_sing$singular], 0)`.
Singular fits also had smaller model SEs. Both features make
their intervals narrower. Coverage among singular fits was
`r fmt_rng(sl_sing$cov[sl_sing$singular])`. Among non-singular
fits it was `r fmt_rng(sl_sing$cov[!sl_sing$singular])`. With
$K - 1$ df, overall coverage was
`r fmt_rng(sl_slope$coverage_km1)`. Under the null, the
random-slopes test had Type I error of
`r fmt_rng(t1_slope$power)` (Table 3). The Discussion,
"Treatment-by-site interaction," takes up the interpretation.

# Discussion

We organize the simulation results around the four research
questions that motivate this study.

**Modeling site effects.** Our findings agree with prior
simulation work [@chu2011comparing; @kahanmorris2013continuous;
@islam2024accounting]. The fixed-site and random-site models
were indistinguishable throughout our grid. Their power differed
by at most `r sprintf('%.3f', hl_fr$d_power)` in any scenario.
This is expected from the design. Every site had about 20
patients, with treatment balanced within site. Treatment is then
nearly orthogonal to site. The fixed model loses only $K - 1$
of about 200 or 600 residual df. In addition, the GLS and OLS
estimators nearly coincide. Our grid therefore cannot show when
one model should be preferred to the other. Earlier work locates
the differences in small centers, many sites relative to $N$,
and low ICC [@pickering2007analysis;
@kahanmorris2013continuous]. None of these regimes was
simulated here. With zero true site variance, the
random-intercept fit was singular in up to
`r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * hl_sing$novar_max)`\% of replicates.
This is expected for REML at a zero variance component. It did
not affect power or coverage in these scenarios.

A further caveat concerns how a random site effect is
justified. It does not concern the simulation's findings. The
design-based argument requires no claim that hospitals are a
random sample of a larger population. In our view it is the
more defensible of the two justifications in the literature.
The full discussion is in the Introduction, "Two different
reasons statisticians give for treating site as random." We
note that ICH E9 does not recommend random site intercepts for
the primary analysis. It mentions mixed models only as a tool
to explore heterogeneity [@iche9, Section 3.2].

**Failure to adjust for stratification.** The 'ignore site'
method in effect represents a failure to adjust for the
stratification variable (site) used in randomization. Under
this method we observed overcoverage and a loss of power. Its
Type I error was well below the nominal level when site
variance was present (Table 2). These results confirm the
findings of Kahan and Morris
[@kahanImproperAnalysisTrials2012a]. That is, when
randomization is stratified by center, the analysis should
account for center. The size of the power penalty depends on
the ICC. With no site-level variance, ignoring site is
harmless. However, the penalty becomes substantial as
$\sigma^2_{\alpha}$ increases.

**Treatment-by-site interaction.** Interaction with
$\sigma^2_{\gamma} = 0.04$ raised the empirical SE of every
method. The random-intercept model does not include the
interaction. Its coverage fell as low as
`r sprintf('%.3f', hl_random$cov_min)`. Its Type I error in the
matching null scenarios rose to
`r sprintf('%.3f', max(t1_fr$power[t1_fr$int]))`. This is
partly a matter of estimand. The fixed-site and random-intercept
models effectively target a weighted average of the effects in
the sampled sites. Against that conditional target, the
fixed-site interval covered at close to the nominal rate
(`r fmt_rng(cond_fixed$coverage_cond)`). The shortfall is
against $\delta$, the mean of the super-population of site
effects. Which target is wanted is a design decision. It should
be stated in advance, following ICH E9(R1) and Kahan and
colleagues [@iche9r1; @kahan2023estimands].

Suppose $\delta$ is the target. Then the random-slopes model
is the appropriate model. Table 3 shows its trade-off. On the one hand,
it raised coverage by up to
`r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * max(sl_cov_gain))` points. Its Type
I error was below, or within Monte Carlo error of, the nominal
level. On the other
hand, it lost
`r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * min(sl_pow_loss))` to
`r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * max(sl_pow_loss))` points of power.
The loss was largest with ten sites. It also returned singular
fits in at least
`r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * min(sl_slope$singular_rate))`\% of
replicates. A singular fit had much larger Satterthwaite df and
lower coverage than a non-singular one. Both halves of the
trade-off matter for practice. Senn argued that some
treatment-by-center interaction is inevitable
[@senn1998controversies]. The power to detect it is typically
low [@sennlewis2019treatment; @iche9]. In our view, researchers
should therefore choose the target and model in advance. They
should not rely on an interaction test.

**Imbalanced site sizes.** We compared balanced and imbalanced
site sizes for the random-intercept model (Figure 3). Without
interaction, imbalance had no consistent effect. The empirical
SE changed by at most
`r sprintf('%.3f', max(abs(bal_diff$d_se[!bal_diff$int])))`.
Power changed by
`r sprintf('%+.1f', 100 * min(bal_diff$d_power[!bal_diff$int]))`
to
`r sprintf('%+.1f', 100 * max(bal_diff$d_power[!bal_diff$int]))`
points, in both directions. This is consistent with Ruvuna and
with Vierron and Giraudeau. They showed that the efficiency loss from unequal
site sizes is small unless the imbalance is extreme
[@ruvuna2004unequal; @vierron2009design]. With interaction,
imbalance raised the empirical SE and lowered power. With
unequal sizes, a few large sites dominate the estimate. Their
realized interaction effects then average out less well. The more
concerning case arises when site size is related to the site
effect. This case is not simulated here. Under informative site
sizes, the patient-weighted and site-weighted average effects
differ [@kahan2023estimands; @neuhaus2006separating].

**Limitations.** We should note that this simulation is
restricted to continuous outcomes analyzed with normal-theory
models. Binary and time-to-event outcomes raise additional
complications. One is separation in fixed effects logistic
regression with many small sites
[@kahanAccountingCentreeffectsMulticentre2014;
@agresti2000strategies; @pickering2007analysis]. The
simulation does not include dropout, non-compliance, or
informative site sizes. The grid keeps about 20 patients per
site with balanced allocation. The ICC values of about 0.09 and
0.33 are high for multicenter trials. As a result, the
fixed-versus-random comparison is uninformative by
construction. The random-slopes comparison covers only six
scenarios and their null counterparts. The mixed models use
Satterthwaite df. We did not evaluate Kenward-Roger df or
methods for very few clusters [@kenward1997small;
@mcneish2016modeling]. Unfortunately, no df method is
guaranteed to be calibrated for singular fits.

# Future research

Several directions merit further investigation:

1. **Random slopes over a full grid.** Our random-slopes
   comparison covers six interaction scenarios and their null
   counterparts. A full factorial over $K$, $n_i$, the ICC, and
   $\sigma^2_\gamma$ would map the trade-off among coverage,
   power, and singular fits. We regard this as
   the most open question in this area.

2. **Small centers, many sites, and low ICC.** Our grid keeps
   about 20 patients per site with balanced allocation. In this
   regime fixed and random site models must nearly agree. The
   methods differ in other regimes [@pickering2007analysis;
   @kahanmorris2013continuous; @mcneish2016modeling]. These
   include small centers ($n_i$ of 2 to 6) with simple
   randomization, $K$ of 50 to 100, and ICC of 0.01 to 0.05.

3. **Non-normal outcomes.** Binary and count outcomes
   require generalized linear mixed models or GEE. The
   relative performance of methods may differ from the
   continuous case. This is particularly likely with sparse
   data per site [@agresti2000strategies;
   @kahanAccountingCentreeffectsMulticentre2014].

4. **Informative site sizes.** Site size may be associated
   with the site-level treatment effect. For example, expert
   centers may enroll more patients and also deliver more
   effective treatment. In that case the patient-weighted and
   site-weighted average effects differ. Standard mixed models
   may then be biased for both [@kahan2023estimands].
   Inverse-probability weighting by site, or joint modeling
   of enrollment and outcome, merit investigation
   [@neuhaus2006separating].

5. **Other small-sample corrections.** We use Satterthwaite
   df for the mixed models, with a $K - 1$ sensitivity
   analysis. Kenward-Roger df [@kenward1997small] and methods
   designed for very few clusters [@mcneish2016modeling] were
   not evaluated. The $K = 10$ random-slopes scenarios deserve
   particular attention. There the slope variance is estimated
   from only ten sites.

6. **Bayesian approaches.** Hierarchical Bayesian models
   offer partial pooling of site-specific treatment effects.
   They may outperform frequentist random effects models when
   the number of sites is very small [@jones1998comparison].

7. **Sample size planning.** Prospective sample size
   calculations could incorporate the design effect from
   multicenter structure. This includes the anticipated ICC
   and site size imbalance. Tools that do so would improve
   trial planning [@vierron2009design;
   @sverdlovSelectingRandomizationMethod2024].

# Data and code availability

All data reported here are synthetic. They are generated by
`analysis/scripts/sim_multicenter.R`. No external or
human-participant data are used. The simulation and reporting
code, including this document's source, are version-controlled
in the repository that contains this report. The simulated data
are reproducible from the fixed seed and RNG kind documented in
Methods ("Simulation procedure"). The function
`build_scenarios()` in the same script defines the exact
scenario grid. We note that a fixed seed and RNG kind alone do
not guarantee identical numeric results across package
versions. The optimizers of `lme4` and `lmerTest` can change
between releases. That behavior bears
directly on the singular-fit diagnostics reported here. The R
package versions are recorded in `renv.lock` at the repository
root. The repository also provides a `Dockerfile` that fixes the
operating system and R build. Neither file controls the BLAS
library or the compiler fully. As a result, small numeric
differences across machines remain possible. The ADEMP
self-audit and its change log are kept in the repository, in
`docs/morris-audit-2026-04-17.md`.
